NOT reverse it. Reversing the counter to start at 7 removes the constant and
breaks the tail -- so a change in the LOOP can flip an allocation in the TAIL,
and the diff points only at the tail.

## Hoisting ONE operand to a local sets evaluation order and operand role INDEPENDENTLY (wave 51, W51-A)

`sub_08053614` merges a shifted field into a masked word:

```
	movs r3, #3
	ands r3, r5
	lsls r3, r3, #0xa      @ the SHIFT is evaluated first
	ldr  r0, =0xFFFFF3FF
	ands r0, r2
	adds r2, r0, #0        @ but the MASKED value is copied into the dest
	orrs r2, r3
```

Thumb `orr` is two-operand, so the destination is a copy of the `|`'s LEFT
operand, while the order the two halves are computed in follows evaluation
order. Written as one expression the two are locked together and each spelling
gets exactly half right: `mask | sh` gives the right operand roles and the wrong
evaluation order, `sh | mask` the reverse. The wave-34 park measured both and
concluded no plain spelling sets them independently -- correct, and the reason is
that the shift is not part of the expression at all:

```c
	s = (b & 3) << 10;
	v.unk04 = (v.unk04 & ~0xc00) | s;
```

The statement boundary fixes evaluation order; the mask stays the left operand
and keeps the destination copy. The hoisted local is dead by the `|` so it costs
no register and does not disturb the value parked across the preceding call.
**Generalised: when a two-operand ALU instruction's operand ROLES and its operand
EVALUATION ORDER disagree with your candidate in opposite directions, hoist the
early-evaluated operand out of the expression rather than swapping the operands.**
This is the "statement boundary is an evaluation-order lever" chapter applied to
the one case where reordering the expression cannot work.

## A descending ADDRESS giv is a real descending source loop -- `check_dbra_loop` only reverses the COUNTER (wave 51, W51-A)

The existing rule says `subs; cmp #0; bge` at a loop bottom does not prove a
descending source loop. True, and it leaves the discriminator unstated. **Read
the ADDRESS, not the counter.** Two twins in this batch clear/copy the same
2 x 8 halfword shape and differ exactly here:

- `sub_08052F3C`: counter runs 7 down to 0, both address givs ASCEND
  (`adds r2,#2; adds r1,#2`). Source is `for (j = 0; j < 8; j++)`; the counter
  was reversed by `check_dbra_loop` and the addresses were not touched.
- `sub_08054B14`: counter runs 7 down to 0 AND the address giv DESCENDS
  (`subs r0,#2`, starting at row+0xe). Source is `for (j = 7; j >= 0; j--)`.

`check_dbra_loop` rewrites the exit test, so it can only ever flip the counter;
it never reverses the direction a giv walks memory. So a descending counter with
an ascending address is a reversed ascending loop, and a descending counter with
a descending address is genuinely descending in the source. Both readings are
free and neither needs a probe.

**REFUTED IN WAVE 59 (W59-E), ON THIS CHAPTER'S OWN SECOND EXAMPLE. A DESCENDING
ADDRESS DOES NOT ESTABLISH A DESCENDING SOURCE, AND THE READING IS NOT FREE.**

`sub_08054B14` matches BOTH WAYS. Both of these compile to the same 64 bytes,
and both were confirmed by exit status from `try_match`, not by eye:

```c
i = 0;                                    for (i = 0; i < 2; i++)
do {                                          for (j = 0; j < 8; j++)
    o = i * 16;  next = i + 1;                    row[i * 8 + j] = 0;
    for (j = 7; j >= 0; j--)
        row[i * 8 + j] = 0;
    i = next;
} while (i < 2);
```

(`row[i * 8 + j]` is shorthand — the literal subscript expression both spellings
use is in `work/sub_08054B14/sub_08054B14.c`, which holds the matched ascending
version. Copy it from there rather than from this block.)

The right-hand spelling ASCENDS and still produces the ROM's descending counter
(`movs r1,#7 ... subs r1,#1; cmp r1,#0; bge`) AND its descending store address
(`strh r3,[r0]; subs r0,#2`, starting at row+0xe). `compile_probe` on it emits a
byte-identical instruction stream to the descending draft, and `try_match`
returns MATCH on both. So `check_dbra_loop` did not merely flip the exit test
here -- when it reversed the counter it RE-BASED the address giv to walk down
with it, which is exactly the thing the paragraph above says it never does.

Caveat on how the measurement was taken, stated so it is not over-read: the two
spellings differ in the outer loop form and in two helper locals as well as in
the inner direction, so this is two matching POINTS rather than a single-variable
ablation. That does not weaken the refutation -- one of the two matching
spellings ascends, which is all it takes -- but it does mean the *cause* is not
isolated. A side result from the same pair: the wave-36 draft's `o = i * 16` and
`next = i + 1` binding locals are NOT load-bearing either; the early
`adds r2, r1, #1` is allocation (r1 is reused as the inner counter), not a source
`next`.

What survives, what does not, and what is now open:

- **Survives:** W37-Q4's rule that a descending COUNTER proves nothing.
- **Does not survive:** "a descending counter with a descending address is
  genuinely descending in the source", at least for a subscripted walk over a
  small constant-trip inner loop. Do not use it as a discriminator.
- **Open:** `sub_08052F3C`'s ASCENDING addresses are still a real difference from
  `sub_08054B14`'s descending ones, and it was not re-tested this wave. Whatever
  separates the twins, it is not source direction, because both source directions
  give `sub_08054B14`'s descending form. Do not read the difference as one.
- **Practical:** when the direction matters, PROBE it rather than arguing from
  the address. At this size that is one `try_match` per direction. Where both
  match, prefer the ascending spelling: it is the more plausible original and it
  needs no helper locals.

### `check_dbra_loop` can DELETE the counter entirely and compare the pointer against the base (wave 51, W51-A)

A third dbra outcome the chapter above does not cover, and it changes the
instruction COUNT rather than just the branch. When an inner loop's index is used
only to address one array through a row pointer and the loop is ASCENDING,
`check_dbra_loop` can drop the counter biv altogether and test the address giv
against the row base:

```
	adds r1, r0, #0
	adds r1, #0xe          @ p = row + 7
L:	strh r3, [r1]
	subs r1, #2
	cmp  r1, r0            @ p >= row   -- no counter anywhere
	bge  L
```

against the counter form the same loop written DESCENDING produces:

```
	movs r1, #7
	...
L:	strh r3, [r0]
	subs r0, #2
	subs r1, #1
	cmp  r1, #0
	bge  L
```

The pointer form is one instruction shorter per iteration, so a ROM carrying the
counter form was **not** written as an ascending loop over a row pointer. More
usefully, the two forms differ in what stays LIVE: the pointer form keeps the row
base live across the whole inner loop as the compare operand, and that extra live
value is enough to evict the outer counter into the inner loop's register,
producing an `adds rN,rI,#1` / `adds rI,rN,#0` copy-back pair around the inner
loop that the counter form does not emit. **So the inner loop's exit-test form
and the OUTER loop's register allocation are one decision, not two** — on
`sub_08054B14` the two spellings each reproduce one half of the ROM exactly and
neither gives both, which is what the function is parked on.

## A `volatile` sub-word READ costs a third register, and the ABSENCE of a dead `ldrb` before a `strb` proves NOTHING (wave 51, W51-B)

`sub_080319AC` sat at 97.50% for six waves on three bytes in one basic block:

    ROM     ldrb r2, [r0, #9] / ldrb r0, [r1] / cmp r2, r0
    draft   ldrb r0, [r0, #9] / ldrb r1, [r1] / cmp r0, r1

The C was already correct — not one character of the body changed. The fix was
a declaration: **`gUnknown_03003F1C` is `volatile u8`.** A volatile QImode read
cannot be folded back into the address register it was loaded through, so it
takes a register of its own and the ROM's operand order falls out. Declared
plain `u8`, each load reuses its own address register and the function misses
by exactly those 3 bytes.

**The reverse inference is the trap, and it had been written into a promoted
file.** `c_08031948.c` argued that because the store to `gUnknown_03003F1C`
carries no dead `ldrb` before its `strb`, while its neighbours do, the global is
NOT volatile. That is wrong. The dead load appears only where the assignment's
VALUE is consumed — a chained assignment such as `a = b = 0;`, which is what
`sub_08032048` records. **A volatile store in statement position, with the value
discarded, is a bare `strb` and is byte-identical to a non-volatile one.** All
five promoted writers of this global (`sub_08030584`, `sub_08031948`,
`sub_08032048`, `sub_08032698`, `sub_08033030`) were re-run with the qualifier
on and are unchanged.

So a volatile qualifier on a scalar global is decided by its READS, never by a
store whose value is thrown away. Where a global has writers only, the honest
header comment is that nothing decides it — which is exactly what the comment
beside `gUnknown_030044C4` already said, and which the later "NOT volatile"
claim contradicted without new evidence.

**Corollary, measured the same wave on `sub_08035170`: `volatile` splits VALUE
CSE but NOT ADDRESS CSE.** Making a struct member's read volatile at the use
site (`*(vu8 *)&g.unk2f`) forces a fresh `ldrb` after an intervening call, but
gcc still keeps the computed address `base + 0x2f` in a callee-saved register
across that call. If the ROM re-derives the *address* as well
(`ldr rB,[rLC]; adds rB,#0x2f; ldrb`), volatile is not the lever you want.

## A permuter run that matches on "raw output" but NOT on "spliced onto the original preamble" is a HEADER REGRESSION — diff the snapshot's declarations (wave 51, W51-B)

This is how the `gUnknown_03003F1C` volatile above was actually found, and it
is a general diagnostic worth reaching for before any hand analysis.

`work/<fn>/permuter/` holds a header-EXPANDED snapshot of the tree, taken when
the function was first imported. It goes stale. `trymatch` checks a permuter
result twice — once spliced onto the current `#include "global.h"` preamble and
once as the raw expanded file — and prints both scores.

- **The two scores AGREE** → the headers have not drifted for this function.
  (Confirmed the same wave on `sub_08035170`: 83.6% both ways.)
- **The two scores DIFFER** → some declaration the function depends on changed
  between the snapshot and now, and the snapshot's version is the one that
  scores better. On `sub_080319AC` the raw form reported `MATCH` while the
  spliced form reported 97.5%, with an identical function body. Diffing the
  snapshot's declarations against the current header named it immediately:
  the snapshot had `extern volatile char gUnknown_03003F1C;`, the tree now had
  `extern u8 gUnknown_03003F1C;`. (`volatile` was the load-bearing half;
  `char` vs `u8` was not.)

The recipe, cheap and mechanical:

    grep -h '^extern ' work/<fn>/permuter/output-*/source.c | sort -u > /tmp/snap
    grep -h '^extern ' include/unknown-globals.h  | sort -u > /tmp/cur
    comm -23 /tmp/snap /tmp/cur

Most hits are cosmetic (whitespace, pool-word globals deleted since), so read
the list for the symbols the function actually touches. **A declaration change
that improves the type model can silently regress a function in a batch nobody
was looking at** — this is the read-side twin of the member-rename trap, and
`proto_check.py` cannot see it either.

## `+3` on the BASE and a two-level `-fforce-addr` word are mutually exclusive — the +3 comes with a LICM hoist (wave 51, W51-B)

`sub_08035080` reads a per-team byte array that lives at `gUnknown_03004490 + 3`
and the ROM does, inside a loop that contains a call:

    ldr r0, [r6]      @ r6 = &.LC ; reload the force-addr word every iteration
    adds r0, #3       @ +3 on the BASE
    adds r0, r4, r0   @ + index

No spelling produces both halves. Measured, each refutes a different theory:

- **`gUnknown_03004490[3 + i]` (array form)** gives the ROM's two-level word —
  pool word holds `&.LC`, `.LC` holds `&gUnknown_03004490`, and the word is
  re-read at every use because the symbol stays a MEM address — but puts the
  `+3` on the INDEX (`adds r0,r5,#3; adds r0,r0,r1`).
- **`((struct T *)gUnknown_03004490)->unk03[i]` (cast form)** puts the `+3` on
  the base, but the cast makes the symbol a pointer VALUE: it gets a ONE-level
  pool word (`.word gUnknown_03004490`, a direct `R_ARM_ABS32` to the symbol)
  and the whole `base + 3` becomes loop-invariant, so LICM hoists it into the
  preheader and the in-loop reload disappears. This is the same behaviour
  `c_08035490.c` relies on, where the ROM *does* hoist.
- **A genuine `struct` VAR_DECL is NOT a third option** — probed directly with
  an `extern struct { u8 f[3]; u8 arr[5]; } g;`. It behaves exactly like the
  cast: `ldr r1,=g; add r1,r1,#3; add r0,r0,r1`, one-level word, hoisted. So
  reshaping the shared `extern u8 gUnknown_03004490[];` declaration would not
  have helped, and the two promoted files that spell it as a cast rather than
  reshaping it were right to.

**Read it as a rule: the runtime `+3` and the un-hoisted reload are the same
fact seen twice.** The base is re-loaded only when it is a MEM the call
invalidates, and a constant offset lands on the base only when the base is a
pointer value — which is precisely when it is *not* such a MEM.

## A NO-OP width cast does not split a CSE (wave 51, W51-B)

Extends the wave-15 probe blind spot to `try_match`. `sub_080363F8` keeps one
value too many live across `__umodsi3`: the ROM keeps only `v.unk04 << 22` and
recomputes `>> 22` afterwards, the candidate keeps both. The obvious lever is to
make the two `(x << 22 >> 22)` sites *different trees* so CSE cannot unify them,
and the cheapest such edit is a cast that is semantically a no-op:

    b->unk04 = (u16)(v.unk04 << 22 >> 22) + ...;

**It changes nothing — byte-for-byte the same output, same +4, same `r9`.** The
value is already known to fit in 10 bits, so the cast is folded away in the
front end, long before CSE ever sees two expressions to compare. If you need to
break a CSE, the two spellings must differ in a way that survives folding; a
width cast that cannot change the value does not.

## A genuine ARRAY_REF expands the BASE first; pointer arithmetic expands the INDEX first (wave 51, W51-D)

`sub_0804C340` and `sub_0804C268` sat at 97.9% / 98.1% for sixteen waves behind a
note that recorded the residual exactly and diagnosed it as unreachable:

```
ROM   ldr  r0, =gUnknown_085D6A48 ; lsls r1, r1, #3 ; adds r1, r1, r0
draft lsls r1, r1, #3 ; ldr  r0, =gUnknown_085D6A48 ; adds r1, r1, r0
```

The note listed four address spellings, all measured byte-identical to each
other, and concluded "the lever is not in the address expression". **All four
were pointer arithmetic** -- `*(u16 *)((u8 *)g + j * 8)`, `((u16 (*)[4])g)[j][0]`,
`((u16 *)g)[j * 4]`, `((struct Row8 *)g)[j].unk00`. Every one of them is a
`PLUS_EXPR` tree, and fold canonicalises `PLUS(addr_const, j * 8)` so the
`MULT_EXPR` becomes operand 0. `expand_expr` then emits operand 0 first, which
is why the shift precedes the base in all four.

**A subscript on a VAR_DECL of ARRAY_TYPE is not a `PLUS_EXPR` at all.** It stays
an `ARRAY_REF`, which `expand_expr` routes through `get_inner_reference`:

```c
    tem = get_inner_reference (exp, ..., &offset, ...);
    op0 = expand_expr (tem, ...);              /* the BASE object, first */
    if (offset != 0)
      offset_rtx = expand_expr (offset, ...);  /* then the offset */
```

Base first, unconditionally, with no fold canonicalisation in between. With
`-fforce-addr` the base's `ldr rN, =sym` is emitted at that point, giving the
ROM's order exactly.

`gUnknown_085D6A48` is declared `u16 [][12]`, so the 8-byte-stride view the two
functions need is spelled **`gUnknown_085D6A48[0][j * 4]`** -- the outer `[0]`
contributes a zero offset and keeps the whole thing an ARRAY_REF on the
VAR_DECL. Both functions matched byte-for-byte on the first attempt with that
one substitution and nothing else changed.

**Rule: when the ROM materialises an array base BEFORE the scaled index, stop
looking for a better cast and find a spelling that keeps the bare symbol as an
ARRAY_REF.** Any cast of the symbol to a pointer type destroys the ARRAY_REF and
locks in the index-first order -- which is why a whole family of casts measures
identical and looks like a dead end.

Corollary, and it is what makes the trap durable: **four spellings agreeing with
each other is evidence they share a mechanism, not evidence the mechanism is
forced.** The note's own measurements were all correct.

## Global allocation order is by LIVE-RANGE LENGTH, and `REG_ALLOC_ORDER` is r3, r2, r1, r0 (wave 51, W51-D)

Measured on `sub_08039F80` by moving one statement and re-reading the assignment
three times. With three competing pseudos and r0/r1 wanted as call scratch:

- The pseudo with the **longest live range is allocated FIRST**, and the first
  allocated gets **r3**, the second r2, the third r1. This is ARM's
  `REG_ALLOC_ORDER = {3, 2, 1, 0, ...}`, so the intuitive reading (first
  allocated gets the lowest number) is backwards.
- So **a register that looks "too high" for a short-lived value means some other
  value's live range is longer than you think**, and the fix is to shorten or
  lengthen a live range, not to reorder statements.

The lever that closed the function was a TYPE change, not an allocation one:

**An `s8`/`u8` local assigned in two places becomes TWO pseudos; an `int` local
stays ONE.** The narrow local's assignment is a truncating copy from the
`do_store_flag` temp, and combine propagates the temp into the single use at
each assignment, leaving the DECL pseudo dead. Two pseudos means two short live
ranges; one pseudo means one long one -- and that is what decides who wins r3.

The tell is in the ROM: `sub_08039F80` holds the same nudge value in **r3 in
both rows**, which one pseudo can do and two cannot. Reading that back:

> **If the ROM uses the SAME register for a value in two disjoint regions, the
> source has ONE variable and it is WIDE. If your candidate uses two different
> registers there, your local is narrow and has been split.**

`int k = c <= 9 ? 0xFC : 0;` with `(s8)k` at each use is byte-identical to
`s8 k = c <= 9 ? -4 : 0;` at the definition (`movs rN,#0xfc`, then
`lsls #0x18; asrs #0x18` at the use) -- the two spellings differ ONLY in how many
pseudos they create. A straight-line probe cannot tell them apart; this is
wave 15's blind spot in its allocation form.

Second half of the same fix: the ROM's `gUnknown_0849D89C` reload in row 2 took
r1, the SHORTEST range. The draft had one function-scope `p` assigned in the
prologue and again in row 2, making it the longest-lived pseudo, which took r3.
Declaring `p` but assigning it **only** in row 2 (letting CSE serve the prologue
and row 1) gave the ROM's r1. **A binding local that spans the whole function
where the ROM's spans one statement is a register-allocation error, not a style
one.**

## `a + 1 + i * 2` reassociates but `a + (i * 2 + 1)` does NOT (wave 51, W51-D)

`sub_08019C40` carried a ruled-out list of eight spellings for one argument --
`a + 1 + i*2`, `1 + a + i*2`, `(a + 1) + i*2`, `a + i*2 + 1`, `i*2 + (a + 1)`,
`a + 1 + 2*i`, `a + 1 + (i << 1)`, `a + 1 + i + i` -- and a correct conclusion
that "the tree agbcc needs is one where fold cannot see the left operand as
`A + constant`". The grouping that does it was not on the list:

```c
(s16)(p->unk4a + (i * 2 + 1))      /* ldrh ; adds #1 ; lsls ; adds  -- the ROM */
(s16)(p->unk4a + 1 + i * 2)        /* lsls ; adds #1 ; ldrh ; adds  -- wrong   */
```

fold's association block splits both operands into var/con/lit parts and only
fires when it finds **more than two** non-empty parts. `(a + 1) + i*2` gives
var0=`a`, lit0=`1`, var1=`i*2` -- three parts, so it associates and the constant
migrates onto the multiply term. `a + (i*2 + 1)` gives var0=`a`, no lit0, and
the whole right side as one part -- **two parts, so association is skipped and
the tree is expanded as written**, left operand first.

This is the opposite of the intuitive reading: writing the constant next to the
term you want it AWAY from is what keeps it where the ROM has it. An explicit
`(s16)` cast on the left operand also works and is byte-neutral here (combine
drops the inner narrowing under the outer one), but the re-grouping is cheaper.

Same function, second residual: **a `negs` sitting with a flag's truncation
rather than with its use means the negation is its OWN source statement.**

```
ROM   ands ; lsls #24 ; lsrs #24 ; negs   ... 13 insns ...   lsrs #31 ; str
```

`flag != 0` on a `u8` local emits `negs; lsrs #31` **adjacent**, at the use.
Splitting it -- `neg = -flag;` as a statement, then `(u32)neg >> 31` in the
argument -- puts each half where the ROM has it. No pass separates that pair, so
a separated pair is always two source statements.

## The `*thumb_andsi3` commutative tie follows which operand DIES, and constant-first is byte-neutral (wave 51, W51-D)

`sub_0805C128` is parked at 98.7% on exactly two bytes:

```
ROM    movs r0,#0xe0 ; ldr r1,=g ; ands r0, r3 ; ldrh r1,[r1] ; cmp r0, r1
draft  movs r0,#0xe0 ; ldr r1,=g ; ands r3, r0 ; ldrh r1,[r1] ; cmp r3, r1
```

`*thumb_andsi3` ties its output to operand 1 with a `%` commutative marker;
`regmove` swaps the operands only when operand 1 does **not** die and operand 2
does. So:

- the **first** AND in that function (`cell & 0x1f`): the cell pseudo is live
  afterwards, the constant dies, the operands swap, and the destination lands on
  the constant's register. ROM and draft agree.
- the **second** AND (`cell & 0xe0`): the cell pseudo dies too. No swap, and the
  destination lands on the cell's register. That is the draft.

For the ROM's choice the cell pseudo must still be LIVE after the AND, and
nothing in the function reads it again.

**Refuted, and it sits in that function's own note as a settled fact: writing the
mask CONSTANT-FIRST (`0xe0 & cell`) is byte-identical to `cell & 0xe0`.** fold
canonicalises a commutative operation with an `INTEGER_CST` operand by moving the
constant to operand 1, so the source order never reaches the RTL. Measured
directly this wave -- same 2 bytes, same 98.7%, same first difference at +0x6e.
The note credited that spelling with fixing 4 of the original 6 bytes; whatever
fixed them, it was not the operand order.

## A returned narrow value costs TWO instructions when it is assigned back to the variable, ONE when it is not (wave 51, W51-F)

The tail of a `u16`-returning function distinguishes `return x + y;` from
`x += y; return x;`, and it is worth 4 bytes. Both narrow, but only the second
writes the variable's own pseudo:

```c
return tile + (len >> 5);     /* lsr r0,r5,#5 ; add r0,r6,r0 ;
                                 lsl r0,r0,#0x10 ; lsr r0,r0,#0x10   */

tile += len >> 5; return tile; /* lsr r0,r5,#5 ; add r0,r6,r0 ;
                                 lsl r0,r0,#0x10 ; lsr r6,r0,#0x10 ;
                                 add r0,r6,#0                        */
```

**The tell is the destination of the second shift.** If the `lsr #0x10` writes
the register the variable has lived in all along and a dead-looking
`adds r0, rV, #0` follows it, the source assigned back and then returned the
variable — the copy is not a scheduling artefact and no allocation lever
removes it. If the `lsr #0x10` writes `r0` directly, the source returned the
expression.

The pseudo is dead immediately either way, which is why this reads as noise;
what keeps it is that the assignment gives the narrowed value a live range
ending at the `return` rather than at the expression. `sub_0805521C` and
`sub_0805530C` are the pair — a probe matched their whole 108/104-byte
instruction streams on the `return x + y;` spelling and was short exactly these
two instructions, and both matched byte-for-byte on the assign-back form with no
other change.

Same family as "binding locals are punctuation" but the opposite direction:
there an extra local BUYS a register, here an extra assignment COSTS two
instructions, and only the ROM's tail says which the original wrote.

## `start_function` WRITES the scaffold `.c` — that is where wave 50's 36 orphan stubs came from (wave 51, W51-F)

`mcp__aw2bhr-decomp__start_function` (and `tools/newfunc.py`) does not just
return a stub in its reply; it creates `work/<fn>/<fn>.c` on disk containing it.
So **surveying a function you then decide not to attempt leaves a compilable
`int f(...) { return 0; }` behind**, which scores 0.0%, is indistinguishable
from a failed draft to the sweep and the next wave's screen, and — the part
that actually bites — makes `trymatch --unit` treat that function as DRAFTED
and try to compile the stub as the real body.

This is the mechanism behind the 36 untouched scaffolds wave 50 found repo-wide.
It is not a bug, but it means:

- **If you call `start_function` on a function you do not go on to draft, delete
  `work/<fn>/<fn>.c` before you finish.** W51-F did exactly this on
  `sub_08079B04`: the unit gate for `sub_0807974C.s` silently dropped from two
  missing drafts to one, which would have made the next agent's job look smaller
  than it is.
- Prefer `get_function` (no assembly, no work directory) for a survey, and
  `start_function` only when the matching attempt actually begins.

## A pure-`goto` loop is INVISIBLE to loop.c — no LICM, no giv, no exit-test duplication (wave 51, W51-G)

gcc 2.x's loop optimiser works from the `NOTE_INSN_LOOP_BEG`/`_END` notes the
front end emits for `for`/`while`/`do`, **not** from the CFG. A loop built only
out of `if`/`goto` carries no such notes, so loop.c never processes it: nothing
is hoisted, no biv/giv is created, and the exit test is not copied into the
preheader.

This is a lever, not a curiosity. `sub_0802C870` (parked wave 42, W42-K) and
`sub_080271CC` (parked wave 38, W38-L) are a twin pair whose park notes recorded
*opposite* symptoms of it — one candidate had the exit test duplicated where the
ROM shared it, the other shared it where the ROM duplicated it. Both ROMs
re-read **both** of their globals on every iteration, and no `while`/`for`/`do`
spelling reproduces that; every one of them lets LICM hoist at least one load
(measured again this wave on four spellings). Rewritten as `goto` loops, both
matched.

**Backwards, as a diagnostic: a loop whose ROM re-loads a global every
iteration, with no giv and no duplicated exit test, was written with `goto`s.**

## A `goto` loop's `-fforce-addr` `.rodata` word is removed by the c_local idiom, NOT by reference count (wave 51, W51-G)

W42-K concluded the lever had to stop the duplication "WITHOUT creating a second
reference site for either global", believing two sites trigger `-fforce-addr`.
**Refuted by probe:** a `goto` loop naming each global exactly ONCE still emits
`.LC` words for both — the level count is a property of the function (W36-L) and
the reference sits at a control-flow merge. Reference count is not the knob.

What removes it is naming the symbol as a POINTER VALUE — binding its ADDRESS to
a local:

```c
struct Unk08499594 **pu = &gUnknown_08499594;   /* ldr r4,=sym  once      */
u16 *pg = &gUnknown_03003F2C;                   /* ldr r3,=sym  once      */
```

giving the ROM's two-level `ldr rN,=sym; ldr rM,[rN]` with the word in the THUMB
text pool. The order these bindings are written in sets the pool word order.

## Scaling the subscript into its OWN local is the only thing that puts the index shifts BEFORE the table's pool load (wave 51, W51-G)

Both ROMs compute `idx * 0xc` and only then load the table pointer. Four
spellings of the subscript were probed and **all four expand the pointer first**
— `(*pu)[idx]`, `(idx + *pu)`, `((T *)((u8 *)*pu + idx * sizeof(T)))->m`, and
the integer-arithmetic form `((T *)(idx * sizeof(T) + (u32)*pu))->m`. The C
front end canonicalises `int + ptr` to `ptr + int` (`pointer_int_sum`), so the
pointer is always op0 and `expand_expr` takes op0 first. A statement boundary is
the only lever:

```c
o = idx * sizeof(struct Unk08499594);
if (((struct Unk08499594 *)((u8 *)*pu + o))->unk00 == 0)
```

This is W36-J's "pre-scaled index local" reached from the other side. Note that
local DECLARATION order does not affect it (three orders probed, all identical).

## A dead `idx = p->m` assignment inside the test is what pins the index to r0 (wave 51, W51-G)

With the three rules above, both functions came out **size-exact and
instruction-exact with r0 and r1 consistently swapped** — the index local wanted
r0 and got r1. The permuter closed both, and its lever was the same each time
and is reusable by hand:

```c
if ((idx = p->unk00) == 0)      /* the store is dead */
```

The dead store extends the index local's live range over the `ldrb`, so the byte
lands in the index's register and the ROM's whole reuse chain
(base -> index -> pointer -> byte, all one register) collapses correctly.
`sub_080271CC` additionally needed `idx = (u16)*pe; idx = idx + i;` split in the
entry copy — that is what ties `adds r0, #1` — plus a separate temp for the loop
copy's byte.

**Do not read the percentage here.** These sat at 84.2% and 88.4% while being
instruction-for-instruction correct; the score was counting register fields.

## Two identical test copies are merged by LATE cross-jumping — two DIFFERENT pointer locals stop it (wave 51, W51-G)

`sub_080271CC`'s ROM carries the array test twice; `sub_0802C870`'s carries it
once with a `b` into the shared tail. **Same source shape.** jump.c's
cross-jumping runs after reload, so two copies merge only if their register
assignments are identical as well. The ROM blocks the merge with
`adds r4, r5, #0`: the entry copy reaches the table through one pseudo and the
loop copy through a second. Reproduced by declaring two `struct Unk08499594 **`
locals and copying one to the other between the entry test and the loop
(`pv = pu;`); the copy survives copy-propagation in that position, where the
same copy written inside a single shared test did not.

## An argument list containing CALLS must not be lifted into locals — `precompute_arguments` keeps the return-value copy (wave 51, W51-J)

Worth 8 bytes and the whole match on both members of the 0807CAFC/080880BC twin
pair, and it is the opposite of the usual advice to bind a subexpression to a
local.

When a call's argument list contains other calls, agbcc runs
`precompute_arguments` over every argument. That path is NOT the same as an
assignment to a local, and it differs in two visible ways:

**1. The return-value copy survives the narrowing.** For
`SetObjAffine(0, Div(...), Div(...), Div(...), Div(...))` where the parameter is
`s16`, the third argument comes out as

    bl Div
    adds r4, r0, #0        <- the copy precompute made
    lsls r4, r4, #0x10
    asrs r4, r4, #0x10

three instructions. Written as `pc = (s16)Div(...);` into an `int` local and
passed as `pc`, combine folds the copy away and you get two:

    bl Div
    lsls r0, r0, #0x10
    asrs r4, r0, #0x10

Same value, one instruction short, and the deficit repeats once per such call.
The copy only shows up where the destination is a LOW register — an argument
that lands in a high register (`mov sl, r0`) needs a move anyway and looks
identical either way, so a probe on those three tells you nothing.

**2. The stack argument is pushed BEFORE the register arguments are loaded.**
With precompute, a five-argument call comes out in textbook order — stack slot
first, then r0, r1, r2, r3:

    lsls r0, r0, #0x10 ; asrs r0, r0, #0x10
    str  r0, [sp]
    movs r0, #0
    mov  r1, sl
    mov  r2, sb
    adds r3, r4, #0
    bl   SetObjAffine

Lift the same values into locals — whether the fifth stays an expression or
becomes a local too — and the register loads move AHEAD of the `str`, because
the pending value is still sitting in r0:

    mov  r1, sl ; mov r2, r8 ; adds r3, r4, #0
    lsls r0, r0, #0x10 ; asrs r0, r0, #0x10
    str  r0, [sp]
    movs r0, #0

Same instruction count, wrong order. **So `str rN, [sp]` immediately after the
last argument's computation, with `movs r0, #imm` following it rather than
preceding it, is a positive tell that the original wrote the arguments inline.**

The same rule reads forwards: `sub_0801A444(a, K, b, f() * 2 + 2)` in
sub_0807CAFC computes a and b into callee-saved registers BEFORE the `bl f`,
then loads r0/r1/r2 after it, which is precompute evaluating arguments left to
right and only then loading the hard registers.

## `-fforce-addr` and LICM are two separate decisions, and const/volatile moves both (wave 51, W51-J)

Measured on sub_08010EF8, which reads one `u16 *` global inside a loop that
stores through a pointer parameter. Four declarations of the same symbol:

| declaration | address handling | the pointer load |
|---|---|---|
| `u16 *const g;` | plain inline pool word | hoisted out of the loop |
| `u16 *g[];` | plain inline pool word | hoisted out of the loop |
| `u16 *volatile g[];` | `.rodata` force-addr word, FOUR levels | hoisted |
| `u16 *g;` (non-const scalar) | `.rodata` force-addr word, FOUR levels | hoisted |

Two things follow, and the second corrects a note left in
`include/unknown-globals.h` in wave 42:

- **The array form does not force-addr where the scalar form does.** A previous
  note generalised "any non-const spelling overshoots to four levels" from
  scalar probes alone; `u16 *g[]` is non-const and keeps the plain inline pool
  word. If you need three levels and not four, that is the spelling.
- **Neither `const` nor `volatile` decides the hoist.** All four rows hoist the
  load, including two that are neither const nor unchanging: agbcc decided a
  store through a pointer parameter cannot alias a static symbol's storage. So
  when a ROM re-reads a global inside a loop and your candidate hoists it, the
  lever is not the global's declaration — it is whatever makes the STORE look
  like a possible alias.

## A one-copy `b` INTO the loop is NOT proof of a `goto` loop — a plain `while` produces it, and the lever is `return` vs `break` (wave 51, W51-K)

`sub_08059E00` is a 60-byte linear search over a 5-entry stack copy. Its ROM
loop is the un-rotated form:

```
	movs r1, #0
_08059E14:
	lsls r0, r1, #1
	add  r0, sp
	ldrh r0, [r0]
	cmp  r4, r0
	bls  _08059E2C            @ the ONLY copy of the test
	adds r0, r1, #1
	lsls r0, r0, #0x18
	lsrs r1, r0, #0x18
	b    _08059E14
```

Three spellings were probed and **all three rotated** — `while (a > v[i]) i++;`,
`for (i = 0; a > v[i]; i++) ;`, and `for (i = 0; ; i++) { if (a <= v[i]) break; }`.
Every one produced a `b` INTO the middle of the loop with **exactly one** copy of
the test, plus a preheader `mov r0, sp` where the first address computation had
const-folded at `i == 0`. That preheader instruction is the whole 2-byte
overshoot; the loop body itself was already right.

The fix is the wave-41 W41-B rule, and nothing else: spell the exit `return`.

```c
    i = 0;
    while (1)
    {
        if (a <= v[i])
            return i + 1;
        i++;
    }
```

Byte-exact first try. **An early exit that jumps to the function epilogue was
written `return`; one that jumps past the loop was written `break`** — including
in the degenerate case where the loop has no other exit, so `break` and `return`
are semantically interchangeable and only the codegen tells them apart.

**This QUALIFIES the wave-46 W46-I chapter above**, which reads a `b` into the
loop with exactly one copy of the test as proof of a label-and-`goto` loop,
"because `loop.c` never sees such a loop at all". W46-I's eight-spelling sweep
was run on a **`volatile`** counter, where agbcc duplicates the test into an
entry guard; on an ordinary non-volatile local it does not, and the one-copy
`b`-into-the-middle form falls straight out of a plain `while`. So:

- W46-I's tell still holds **where the loop counter is `volatile`** — that is
  the case it was measured on, and the flash delay loops are all of that kind.
- Where it is not, **read the one-copy form as ordinary rotation** and reach for
  `return`/`break` before you reach for `goto`. A `goto` loop is the expensive
  hypothesis and it was not needed here.

## A big constant stored to a NARROW lvalue costs an extra move — route it through an `int` (wave 51, W51-K)

`sub_08059C00`'s only residual was one instruction, and it was this.

```c
    out[0] = 0x270f;        /* out is u16 * */
```

agbcc materialises the constant in HImode and then copies it:

```
	ldr  r1, =0x270F
	add  r0, r1, #0          @ not in the ROM
	strh r0, [r5]
```

Spelling the store `*out = …`, casting the lvalue to `s16 *`, and casting the
constant `(u16)0x270f` all produce the identical pair — the lvalue is not the
variable. Assigning through an `int` is:

```c
    t = 0x270f;             /* int t */
    out[0] = t;
```

```
	ldr  r0, =0x270F
	strh r0, [r5]
```

which is the ROM. The constant stays SImode, and combine folds the truncation
into the `strh`, where an HImode constant needs its own materialisation first.

**The threshold is what makes this readable in reverse.** The same function
stores `0x7fff` to an `s16` member two instructions later with no extra move,
because CSE hands that store the register the preceding comparison already
loaded. So the cost only appears for a constant whose **first** use in the
function is a narrow store, and only when it is too large for a `movs` imm8.

**Do not reach for this before the rest of the stream is aligned.** It is worth
exactly 2 bytes and it looks like a register-allocation diff, which is the
family of error waves 16 and 18 recorded: a lever that appears to work may be
paying for something wrong elsewhere. Here everything else was already exact.

## A five-byte clear that runs BACKWARDS in the ROM was written FORWARDS — and the pointer form is distinguishable (wave 51, W51-M)

Two functions in this batch end on the same idiom, `sub_08088044` for
`gUnknown_03005978` and `sub_0807C588` for `gUnknown_03005910`:

```
	ldr r1, =gUnknown_03005978
	movs r2, #0
	adds r0, r1, #4
_loop:
	strb r2, [r0]
	subs r0, #1
	cmp r0, r1
	bge _loop
```

The counter IS the pointer, it walks down, and there is no entry guard. The
obvious reading — a descending pointer loop — is wrong twice over, and both
wrong readings cost an attempt:

- `for (p = &a[4]; p >= a; p--) *p = 0;` adds a **zero-trip guard**
  (`subs r1,r0,#4; cmp r0,r1; bcc`) and makes both compares **UNSIGNED**
  (`bcc` / `bcs`), because two pointers of unknown value compare unsigned. It
  was +4 bytes on one function and +16 on the other.
- `for (i = 4; i >= 0; i--) a[i] = 0;` keeps `i` as the biv and recomputes the
  address every iteration (`adds r0, r1, r3`), which is a different stream
  again.

What produces the ROM exactly is the **ascending** loop:

```c
for (i = 0; i < 5; i++)
    gUnknown_03005978[i] = 0;
```

`check_dbra_loop` reverses it, and because the index has no surviving use it
replaces the biv with the address giv and rewrites the exit test against the
array base. The signedness is the tell and it is decisive: the reversed test
inherits the source's **signed** `i >= 0`, so it comes out `bge`, where any
pointer comparison you write yourself comes out `bcc`/`bcs`. **`bge` on two
addresses means the source compared an `int`, not two pointers** — and the
absent entry guard means the bounds were constants the compiler could see.

Both functions matched on the attempt that switched to the ascending form.

## Reading a SIGNED byte out of a `u8 *` table: where the copy lands tells you which spelling (wave 51, W51-M)

`sub_08059050` reads `gUnknown_03003340[y][x]`, declared `u8 *[]`, with an
`ldrsb` and tests it `< 0`. Two spellings both produce the `ldrsb`, and they
differ by exactly one instruction:

```c
s8 v = g[y][x];  if (v >= 0 && v < *best)     /* ONE pseudo */
if ((s8)g[y][x] >= 0) { v = g[y][x]; ... }    /* TWO pseudos */
```

The first coalesces the load with `v` and reads `ldrsb rV,[rA,rZ]` straight
into `v`'s register. The second leaves the load in a scratch, tests the
scratch, and copies it to `v` with `adds rV, rLOAD, #0` — which is what the
ROM does, because the scratch is then needed for the `ldrsh` of `*best`. **A
surviving `adds rV, rLOAD, #0` between a load's test and its later use means
the test read the EXPRESSION and the variable was assigned separately.** It is
the same two-pseudo mechanism the `t = X; if (f(X))` note records, seen from
the load side.

The cast is also load-bearing for a different reason: `-Werror` rejects
`g[y][x] >= 0` outright ("comparison is always true due to limited range of
data type") because the declared element is unsigned. **An always-true warning
on a `< 0` test is evidence the original table was declared SIGNED** — the
cast is how you keep the shared `u8 *` declaration and still compile.

## To get `fold` to move a member offset into the base, the member must be REAL — a cast on the base blocks it (wave 51, W51-M)

W35-F records that a local struct view STOPS `fold` reassociating a
base-plus-constant. This is the same fact from the other side, and it decides
whether you cast or edit the header.

`sub_08055288` reads a length at +0 and a source pointer at +4 out of one
20-byte row, and the ROM keeps the two accesses APART:

```
	adds r1, r0, r3      @ r3 = =gUnknown_08553D80, r0 = the shared byte offset
	ldrh r4, [r1]
	adds r3, #4          @ the address constant gUnknown_08553D80 + 4
	adds r0, r0, r3
	ldr r0, [r0]
```

`fold` pulled the `+4` out of the inner sum and into the address constant, so
the two members share the OFFSET and not the address. Reaching the rows
through a cast — `((const struct Row (*)[5])&gUnknown_08553D80)[v][c].unk04` —
does not reproduce it: the `NOP_EXPR` stops the reassociation, gcc CSEs the
whole element address instead, and the second access becomes a displacement,
`ldr rD,[rB,#4]`. That is **4 bytes short**, and no local, statement boundary
or operand reordering recovers it.

The genuine member spelling `gUnknown_08553D80.unk00[v][c].unk04` produces the
ROM. So when a shared struct's `filler` turns out to hold a real array, the fix
is to NAME it in the header rather than cast around it — and it can be done
without touching anything below, by declaring the member with the extent that
makes it stop exactly where the next named member starts (here
`struct Unk08553D80Row unk00[1][5];` plus `filler_64[0x04]`, ending at 0x68).
The outer extent is a floor, not a bound; the subscript is a run-time value and
the rows plainly continue past it. `sub_0805521C` is the matched exemplar for
the same idiom on a table that was already declared this way.

## Binding a STACK-PASSED parameter to a local can buy a register AND kill a competing LICM hoist (wave 52, W52-A)

`sub_0800401C` takes five parameters, so `t` arrives at `[sp,#0x28]`. Written
naturally, agbcc left it in memory and reloaded `ldr r2,[sp,#0x28]` at both
call sites inside the doubly-nested loop — *and*, having a register spare,
LICM-hoisted `&gUnknown_08499590` into `sl`, which the ROM does not do (the ROM
re-emits `ldr r0,=gUnknown_08499590 ; ldr r0,[r0] ; ldrh` at both read sites off
one shared pool word).

Adding a single `tt = t;` at the top fixed **both** at once: the parameter got a
callee-saved register and the address hoist disappeared, because the hoist was
only ever there to spend a register nothing else was claiming.

Read this as the register-pressure rule of the `.rodata` chapter run
**backwards**. That chapter says a draft carrying *more* live values than the
original emits a pool the ROM does not have. The mirror is just as diagnostic:
**a draft that HOISTS an address the ROM rematerialises is carrying FEWER live
values than the original**, and the fix is to find the value the original is
keeping in a register and give it one.

- The lever is specific to *stack-passed* parameters. It does nothing for a
  register parameter: `hh = h;` on the 4th parameter was byte-identical, because
  agbcc copy-propagates the binding straight back to the incoming `r3` and `hh`
  never becomes a distinct allocno. Do not reach for it as a general
  allocation lever — see "BINDING LOCALS ARE PUNCTUATION".

## Splitting an address expression into statements does NOT block agbcc's fold (wave 52, W52-A)

The intuition that separate C statements survive to RTL is right for masks (see
the two-`ands` rule above) and **wrong for shift/add address arithmetic**.
`sub_080029F4`'s ROM computes `((a1 - 1) * 8 + 0x28C) * 32 + 0x06010000` with
every step separate, in one basic block:

```
subs r1,r6,#1 ; lsls r1,r1,#3 ; movs r2,#0xa3 ; lsls r2,r2,#2
adds r1,r1,r2 ; lsls r1,r1,#5 ; ldr r2,=0x06010000 ; adds r1,r1,r2
```

Four spellings were measured and **all four collapse to the same three
instructions** (`lsls r1,r6,#8 ; ldr r2,=0x06015080 ; adds r1,r1,r2`):

| spelling | result |
|---|---|
| one expression with `* 8` | folded |
| one expression with `<< 3` | folded |
| `idx = (a1-1)*8 + 0x28C;` then `idx*32 + base` at the use | folded |
| `idx = a1-1; idx = idx*8; idx = idx+0x28C;` then `idx*32 + base` | folded |

combine's `simplify_shift_const` distributes the shift over the `+ 0x28C` and
then over the `- 1`, reassembling the chain through the LOG_LINKS however the
source splits it. The two-`ands` rule does not transfer because 0x28C is
`movs #0xa3; lsls #2`-representable and therefore stays a bare `CONST_INT`
rather than becoming the `(mem (label_ref))` that starves combine.

**So the shift/multiply case needs the intermediate to have a SECOND REFERENCE
or to cross a control-flow merge — a statement boundary is not enough.** The
exemplar `sub_08002964` gets its unfolded `idx << 5` for exactly that reason:
its `idx` is assigned in both arms of an `if` and read after the join.

## An OPEN case: a dead sign-extended byte load the ROM emits and no dead local reproduces (wave 52, W52-A)

`sub_080079B8` (84 B) and `sub_080077EC` (232 B) both contain this, and in both
the result is clobbered by the very next instruction:

```
adds r0,#0x36 ; ldrb r0,[r0] ; lsls r0,#0x18 ; asrs r0,#0x18 ; adds r0,#4
...
lsls r0, r2, #3          <- r0 overwritten, value never used
```

It is `(s8)p->unk36 + K` where `K` is the same constant the *live* index takes
from `p->unk3a` two members over, and in `sub_080079B8` it is also the last use
of `p`, which is why the ROM spends `adds r0,#0x36` on the pointer register.
`sub_080077EC` has a compiler-generated jump table, so this is agbcc output.

A plain dead local does **not** reproduce it — the whole `if`/`else` disappears
and the function loses its prologue with it, confirming the existing
"a dead assignment to a local buys nothing at all" rule for this shape. The
untried vehicles, in the order worth trying: a dead **store to memory** that DSE
removes while store-forwarding keeps the value (the `sub_08067F5C` asymmetry
recorded earlier in this file is the only documented construct that leaves a
computation standing), a struct-member store overwritten by a later one, or a
`volatile` lvalue. A `volatile` *local* is ruled out: it needs a stack slot and
both ROM frames are `push`-only.

## Binding a plane byte to a local flips reload's commutative AND tie

Wave 52, W52-C. Measured on three functions in one batch, and it closed
`sub_0805C128` after that function had sat at 98.7% for two waves with a draft
note recording the opposite as settled.

When a byte read out of memory feeds **only bitwise masks**, do NOT bind it to a
local. Name the member at each mask site:

```c
t = map->unk1432[idx] & 0x1f;                    /* named twice */
if (tbl[t] != 0 && (0xe0 & map->unk1432[idx]) != g)
```

Both spellings emit **one** `ldrb` — CSE merges the loads — so the choice is
invisible in the instruction count and shows up only as which operand of
`*thumb_andsi3` reload ties the destination to:

```
    two named reads   movs r0,#0xe0 / ands r0, r3      <- the ROM
    `u8 cell` local   movs r0,#0xe0 / ands r3, r0      <- 2 bytes wrong
```

The mechanism is reload's commutative `%` swap, which ties the destination to
the input that **dies** at the insn. A bound local makes the last mask the last
use of a one-reference pseudo, so the byte dies there and takes the destination.
Two named reads give the value two references, the constant dies first, and the
destination goes to the constant's register — the ROM's choice.

`sub_08059E3C` shows the identical flip on the identical `& 0x1f` / `& 0xe0`
pair over the same +0x1432 plane byte, so this is the pair's shape, not one
function's accident.

**It is not "never bind".** `sub_08059F24`, in the same batch and over the same
map, *requires* the binding: there the byte also feeds a `* 12` and a `strh`,
and the unbound form CSEs the address but reloads the value across the
intervening branches (`ldrb r2,[r2]`) and sinks the pool pointer load above the
multiply. The rule that fits all three:

- byte feeds masks only → name the member at each use;
- byte feeds anything else (arithmetic, a store, an array subscript) → bind it.

Also ruled out for this tie, both by probe: `int cell` holding the raw byte with
a second narrow local for the code (96.1%, worse — the SImode pseudo *also*
sinks the pool `ldr` below the `ands`), and `(u8)(0xe0 & cell)`, which is the
wave-15 probe trap already recorded in `work/sub_0805C128/`.

## A store through a POINTER PARAMETER does not kill a global pointer's load

> **SOLVED IN WAVE 59 — read "ONE untraceable store anywhere in a loop is the
> LICM barrier" at the end of this file before spending anything here.** Every
> measurement below is correct and none of it is retracted. What was wrong was
> this chapter's closing question, which asks what makes the CURSOR opaque; the
> cursor is the wrong object. One untraceable store *anywhere* in the loop is
> enough, and `gUnknown_03003340[y][x] += 0;` — a store through a row pointer
> loaded from memory, dead, deleted before output, zero bytes — took
> `sub_08059F24` from 31.6% / +4 to 87.3% / size-exact by itself.
> `sub_08059F24` and `sub_0805A008` are MATCHED; `sub_08059E3C` is at 98.3%.

Wave 52, W52-C. Two eight-line probes, identical but for the store target,
compiled side by side:

```c
void t1(u8 *out)   { for (y=0; y<*(u16*)(g+2); y++) for (x=0; x<*(u16*)g; x++) *out++ = x; }
void t2(void)      { for (y=0; y<*(u16*)(g+2); y++) for (x=0; x<*(u16*)g; x++) gUnknown_03003340[y][x] = x; }
```

`t1` loads `gUnknown_08499590` **once**, in the duplicated loop guard, and keeps
it in a callee-saved register for both loop tests. `t2` re-reads it at every
test. The only difference is the pointer the `strb` goes through: an incoming
**parameter** in `t1`, a pointer **loaded from memory** in `t2`.

This is the mechanism behind `src/decomp/c_0801F838.c`'s comment ("both bounds
are re-read every iteration because the `strb` goes through a pointer the
compiler cannot see past"), which had recorded the effect without the cause. It
also explains why `c_0805A268.c` and `c_0805A514.c` match with either spelling:
they contain `bl`s, and a `CALL_INSN` sets `unknown_address_altered` and kills
the load regardless.

**Read it as a diagnostic.** If your candidate hoists a global pointer that the
ROM re-reads at each loop test, the difference is not register allocation — it
is that the original's loop wrote through something opaque and yours does not.
The cached value is expensive: in `sub_08059F24` it costs two callee-saved
registers (the map pointer *and* `&gUnknown_08499590`), which spills the
loop-invariant `y * 2` to a stack slot for +4 bytes and denies another global
the register the ROM hoists it into.

**Open, and worth 688 bytes.** `sub_08059F24`, `sub_0805A008` and
`sub_08059E3C` all store through what is plainly the r0 parameter
(`adds r3, r0, #0`) and yet the ROM re-reads the map pointer at every test. So
some spelling makes a parameter-based emit opaque and it is not yet known.
Ruled out by probe, none moving the cache by one instruction: struct-member vs
flat `u8 *` / `*(s16 *)` stores (so not `MEM_IN_STRUCT_P`, and not TBAA — `u8`
is `unsigned char`, alias set 0, which conflicts with everything anyway);
`out++` vs `out[n]` with a counter; and the W34-F COMPONENT_REF spelling vs flat
pointer arithmetic.

**Wave 57, W57-B — the STORE TYPE axis is dead, and the discriminator is the
BASE.** Five one-loop probes differing only in what is stored through:

```c
void probeA(u8 *out)   { for (y=0;y<*(u16*)(g+2);y++) out[y] = y; }   /* hoists */
void probeB(char *out) { ... }                                        /* hoists */
void probeC(u16 *out)  { ... }                                        /* hoists */
void probeD(u8 **out)  { ... }                                        /* hoists */
void probeE(void)      { for (...) gUnknown_030045F0[y] = y; }        /* RELOADS */
```

A–D are byte-identical in this respect: **every** store type through a pointer
parameter caches the global, including `u8 **`, whose alias set is exactly the
global's own. So this is not TBAA in either direction, and the tempting
"`unsigned char` may not get alias set 0 in agbcc, try `char`" hypothesis is
refuted — `char` caches too. `probeE` differs only in that its store base is a
**global array** rather than a parameter, and it reloads at every test, which is
the ROM's pattern. The axis is `base_alias_check`'s argument/stack-base rule:
an argument-derived base is treated as aliasing nothing, whatever is stored
through it. Do not spend further probes on the stored type.

This makes the open problem sharper, not solved: the ROM's cursor **is** the r0
parameter, so on this rule it should cache and does not. What is left to test is
something that makes the cursor's base untraceable to an argument, or a
non-aliasing cause (CSE path/allocation) entirely.

**The residual is now measured exactly.** Rebuilt from `c_0805A388.c`'s spelling,
`sub_08059E3C`'s body is byte-identical to the ROM and the whole diff is **two
instructions**, both the same thing: the inner loop guard and the outer latch
read the cached pointer (`mov r0, r8`) where the ROM re-reads it (`mov r1, ip;
ldr r0, [r1]`). That is the entire -4. `sub_08059F24` / `sub_0805A008` are the
same fault plus its knock-on spill. Anyone testing a new hypothesis should use
`sub_08059E3C` — it is the cleanest instrument in the tree for this bug.

**Two levers that ARE settled for these three, worth keeping:** in
`sub_08059F24` the `+0x12` cell byte **must** be bound to a `u8` local. Named at
each of its four uses it reloads the value across the branches (`ldrb r2,[r2]`
before the `*12`) and sinks the `gUnknown_08499594` pool load above the
multiply; bound, both go away and the two masks land on the ROM's operand ties
(`ands r0,r2` on the non-final `& 0xc0`, `ands r2,r0` on the final `& 0x3f`).
`sub_08059E3C` is the opposite and stays unbound, exactly as
`src/decomp/c_0805C128.c` records. Also: the `0xFFFF` terminator must be stored
through the `s16` struct member — as `*(s16 *)(out + 2) = 0xFFFF` on a flat
`u8 *` cursor agbcc builds the constant with `movs #1; neg; add` instead of the
ROM's pool word.

**A W34-F footnote measured along the way:** for these map readers
`((struct Map *)gUnknown_08499590)->unit[off]` and c_0805A388.c's flat
`q = gUnknown_08499590; props = q + 0x12; props[off]` are **byte-identical**,
for the plane addresses and for the loop guards alike. W34-F reads as though the
flat spelling always costs something; it does not, and both promoted styles are
fine.

## A dead store through a GLOBAL-DERIVED pointer is a ZERO-BYTE LICM barrier — and it is the missing third case (wave 52, W52-B)

This closes the question the W50-L / W51-C pair leaves open. Their result was:
`symbol` vs `symbol` and `symbol` vs *parameter*-derived pointer are both
disambiguated (six spellings of the out-pointer all hoist), while
`symbol` vs `symbol[variable]` is not.

`sub_0805A6DC` is the third case and it behaves like the second, not the first:

```c
for (i = gUnknown_03003F2C; i < gUnknown_03003F2C + 0x40; i++)
{
    u = &gUnknown_08499594[i];   /* u is derived from the pointer GLOBAL */
    u->unk03 += 0;               /* <-- dead store. LOAD-BEARING. */
    ...
    *out = u->unk02;             /* stores through the u8 * PARAMETER */
    ...
}
```

Without the `+= 0` line, agbcc hoists **both** `gUnknown_08499594` (a pointer
global) and the bound `gUnknown_03003F2C` (a `u16` scalar global) out of the
loop; `check_dbra_loop` then reverses the loop into a countdown (`subs r2,r4,r2`
trip count in the preheader, `subs; cmp #0; bne` at the bottom) and the function
comes out **4 bytes short**. The ROM instead reloads both every iteration and
keeps `i` as a real biv. With the `+= 0` it is byte-for-byte identical.

Three things make this worth a chapter:

* **It costs zero bytes.** `prescan_loop`'s `note_addr_stored` records the store
  and that is enough to make `invariant_p` return 0 for every MEM in the loop;
  the store itself is dead and is deleted again before output. So the barrier is
  free, unlike every other lever in this file.
* **The out-pointer is irrelevant, confirming W51-C.** The cursor was tried as
  `struct Unk5A514Cell *` with `out->x`/`out->y`/`out->v` (48.1%, -4) and as a
  plain `u8 *` with flat derefs (52.9%, size-exact). Neither blocks the hoist.
  Only a store whose lvalue reaches through the *global* does. Do not retype the
  out-pointer to chase this; wave 48, wave 51 and now wave 52 have each paid for
  that lead.
* **A `for (i = g; i < g + 0x40; i++)` scan over `gUnknown_08499594[i]` is
  therefore NOT self-similar across the 0x0805A block.** `sub_0805A514` and
  `sub_0805A5E0` reload because they *call out* (the note on
  `gUnknown_03003F2C` in include/unknown-globals.h says exactly this);
  `sub_08057F00`/`F54`/`FA8` hoist because they have no stores at all;
  `sub_0805A6DC` has neither a call nor a global-derived store, and is the one
  that needs the barrier written by hand. Decide which of the three you have
  before writing the loop.

Found by decomp-permuter in 68 iterations after five hand attempts had missed
it. **If a loop-form residual is exactly ±4 bytes and the diff shows the ROM
re-reading a global you hoisted, try this before anything else.**

## `(&p[i])->m[k]` and `p[i].m[k]` are DIFFERENT CODE (wave 52, W52-B)

They are the same C and the same tree to a reader, and agbcc emits different
register assignments for them. On `sub_08059B4C`:

```c
arr = gUnknown_084995A0;
if (n < (&arr[w])->unk03[k]) goto loop;   /* MATCH */
if (n < arr[w].unk03[k])      goto loop;  /* 97.8%, 4 bytes */
```

The member form swaps r0/r1 around the `ldrsb` that produces `w` and moves the
pool `ldr` relative to it. **Do not "tidy" an ARRAY_REF-of-address form the
permuter hands you into the member form** — that is exactly how a verified match
gets silently regressed during cleanup, and it happened once in this wave before
being caught by re-running `try_match` on the cleaned file. Re-verify after
every cosmetic edit to a matched draft.

Same function, same wave, a second placement rule that goes with it: **bind the
pointer global in its OWN statement, after the value that indexes it is
computed.** Written in place as `&gUnknown_084995A0[w]`, the pool `ldr` is
scheduled between the pointer global's two loads; bound as `arr = ...` on its
own line after `w = *(s8 *)(cells + idx);`, the two loads stay adjacent as the
ROM has them. This is the W43-I "give it its own statement" rule, and the
ordering half of it matters as much as the binding half.

## `dst[off - k]` and `*(dst + off - k)` are DIFFERENT CODE — and both arms of an `if`/`else` must use the SAME form (wave 52, W52-B)

`sub_0805772C` writes a 7-tile digit strip either forwards or mirrored:

```c
if (par != 0)
    for (k = 6; k >= 0; k--) *(dst + off - k) = ...;
else
    for (k = 0; k <= 6; k++) *(dst + off + k) = ...;
```

The subscript form `dst[off - k]` builds the giv's initial value as
`plus(off * 2, dst)`; the explicit pointer form binds `dst + off` as a
subexpression first and builds `plus(dst, off * 2)`. Those are different
`adds rD, rN, rM` encodings — `adds r0, r7, r2` against `adds r0, r0, r7` — and
they cascade into which register `off` itself lands in, four spots downstream.

**The mixed spelling is worse than either pure one.** With the mirrored arm as
`*(dst + off - k)` and the forward arm still `dst[off + k]`, the function sat at
94.6% with the residual entirely in the *forward* arm. Converting the forward
arm to `*(dst + off + k)` as well matched it. The two arms are mutually
exclusive and share only `off`, so this is not an aliasing or CSE effect — the
association gcc picks for one arm's giv init constrains the register `off` gets,
which the other arm then has to live with. **When an `if`/`else` writes the same
buffer two ways, spell both index expressions identically.**

## The "flat off the symbol" spelling controls WHERE the symbol's `ldr` lands in the preheader — but never with a constant added to the symbol (wave 52, W52-B)

Extends the W48-I chapter on preheader order. In `sub_080564B8`,
`gUnknown_02029816[a2][i] = 1;` and
`*(u16 *)(a2 * 0x6c + i * 2 + (char *)gUnknown_02029816) = 1;` produce the same
loop body and different **preheaders**:

```
subscript form:  ldr r6,=sym / movs r0,#0x6c / adds r2,r4,#0 / muls r2,r0,r2 / movs r5,#1
flat form:       movs r0,#0x6c / adds r2,r4,#0 / muls r2,r0,r2 / ldr r6,=sym / movs r5,#1  <-- ROM
```

The subscript form's tree is `(&arr + a2 * 0x6c) + i * 2`, so the symbol's
pseudo is created first and LICM emits it first. The flat form's is
`(a2 * 0x6c + i * 2) + sym`, which creates it last. Worth 12 of the 22 differing
bytes here, in two preheaders at once.

**The trap:** the same reassociation with a CONSTANT added to the symbol —
`(char *)gUnknown_02029808 + 0xe` — is folded at compile time into the pool word
itself, emitting `.word gUnknown_02029808+0xe` where the ROM has
`.word gUnknown_02029808` plus a runtime `adds r2,#0xe` (cse.c's
`use_related_value`, per W49-D). So the flat form is available only when nothing
constant is added to the symbol; for a member row, keep the member spelling and
move the *index* instead.

## A permuter match that holds only for "raw permuter output (headers expanded)" means the randomizer changed a DECLARATION (wave 52, W52-B)

`trymatch` checks a permuter result two ways — spliced onto the original
preamble, and as the raw header-expanded file. When those two **disagree**, the
body is not what closed it: something in the expanded headers differs from what
`global.h` gives, and decomp-permuter's randomizer edits type qualifiers.

On `sub_08059B4C` the expanded file carried

```c
extern volatile int gUnknown_03004788;
```

and that is a real finding, not an artefact. The ROM holds the symbol's address
in r2 and issues a second `ldr r1,[r2]` for `if (a2 > g) a2 = g;`; non-volatile,
CSE always folds the assignment to `adds r1,r0,#0`, and no spelling of the
statement (plain `if`, `?:`, a temporary, two divides relying on cross-jumping)
prevents it. The `volatile` was moved into include/unknown-globals.h with the
evidence, the only other reader (`sub_08061CF8`) was re-verified byte-exact, and
the function then matched from the ordinary preamble.

**So: diff the permuter's expanded preamble against the header before assuming a
splice failure is a harness bug.** `grep` the output's `extern` line for each of
the function's `data_refs`. This is the cheapest volatile-detector the project
has — the randomizer searches a space hand analysis does not.

## A MASK CONSTANT is emitted after its operand and ties the result to the operand — unless you give it its own statement (wave 52, W52-E)

Two near-misses that had each stood for two waves, `sub_08066EBC` (96.0%) and
`sub_08023BAC` (98.9%), were the same fact seen from two sides, and both closed
by moving a constant out of an expression and into a statement of its own.

**The mechanism.** For `x & K` with `K` an `INTEGER_CST`, two things happen and
neither is reachable by rewriting the expression:

1. `fold` canonicalises the constant to tree operand 1, and `expand_expr`
   expands operand 0 first. So the OPERAND's instructions are emitted before the
   constant's `mov`, and **`K & x` and `x & K` produce byte-identical code**.
2. `expand_binop` is then free to reuse operand 0's register as the target, so
   the result ties to the OPERAND's register: `ands rOperand, rConst`.

THUMB has no AND-immediate, so `K` needs a register either way — which is why
this is invisible until you diff the register names.

**The lever is a statement boundary, and it works in both directions.**

*Constant needed FIRST (`sub_08066EBC`).* The ROM had `movs r1,#15` before
`lsrs r0,r4,#1`. Assigning the mask to a plain local in its own statement puts
the `mov` where the statement is, and cse does not fold it back into the `and`
because the constant has to occupy a register regardless:

```c
m = 0xf;
i = (u32)gUnknown_03004008 >> 1;
i &= m;                  /* mov r1,#0xf ; lsr r0,r4,#1 ; and r0,r1  -- MATCH */
```

Measured against it, all emitting the shift first: `((u32)g >> 1) & 0xf`,
`0xf & ((u32)g >> 1)`, `((u32)g >> 1) % 0x10`, and a two-statement
`i = (u32)g >> 1; i &= 0xf;`.

*Tie needed on the CONSTANT (`sub_08023BAC`).* The ROM had `ands r1, r0` with
r1 holding the mask. Here the fix is not to name the constant but to **split the
u16 widening from the mask**, which routes the whole thing through `combine`
instead of `expand`:

```c
a1 = a1 + 2;
a1 &= 0x1F;              /* add r0,r7,#2 ; lsl r0,#16 ; mov r1,#0xf8 ;
                            lsl r1,#13 ; ands r1,r0 ; lsr r7,r1,#16  -- MATCH */
```

The u16 assignment emits its own `lsl #16; lsr #16` pair, combine folds the mask
through it into `(lshiftrt (and (ashift x 16) 0x1f0000) 16)`, and the constant
is `force_reg`'d **at the combined insn** — a later pseudo, which wins the tie.
Ruled out by probe, all with identical surrounding code:

- `(((a1 + 2) << 16) & 0x1F0000) >> 16` — the honest transcription of the six
  instructions. Right instructions, wrong tie (`ands r0, r1`). This is what the
  function carried at 98.9%.
- `mask = 0x1F0000;` in its own statement *before* the value — right tie, wrong
  order, because the mask pair is now emitted first.
- `t2 = (a1+2) << 16; mask = 0x1F0000; a1 = (t2 & mask) >> 16;` — right order,
  still `and r0, r0, r1`. **Naming the constant is not sufficient**; the
  widening has to be a separate statement so combine builds the insn.
- `a1 = (u16)(a1 + 2) & 0x1F;` — collapses to `add; mov #0x1f; and`.

**Read this backwards as a diagnostic:** if a diff's only fault is which side of
an `ands`/`orrs`/`adds` the result landed on, do not reach for the permuter and
do not chase the allocator. Ask which operand was a literal in your source and
whether the original wrote it as its own statement. Compare the sibling rule for
`|` at "OPERAND ORDER inside a commutative `|`".

## The permuter closes an allocation swap between INDEPENDENT locals and does not close one between the ARMS OF A TERNARY (wave 52, W52-E)

Both were run the same wave, both from an instruction-exact, size-exact,
correct-order candidate — the case the permuter documentation calls its own —
and they came out opposite ways.

| function | residual | result |
|---|---|---|
| `sub_08022428` | `cx`/`cy`, two independent locals, swapped between r9 and sl | **matched at iteration 553** |
| `sub_08028EF0` | `a`/`abs_b`, the two arms of one ternary, swapped between r1 and r2 | nothing in ~18,935 iterations |

`sub_08028EF0` has now had ~40,000 iterations across two different starting
points (21,155 in wave 42 from a 96.6% draft, ~18,935 in wave 52 from the
instruction-exact one), so "try a different starting point" is spent on it.

**The discriminator is whether the two values have independent definitions the
randomizer can reorder.** `sub_08022428`'s `cx` and `cy` are two separate
assignment statements, and swapping them is a legal source permutation that
flips pseudo-creation order — for the record, doing it by hand also flips r9/sl
correctly but swaps the two `ldrh` loads, which is why the tool beat the hand
fix. `sub_08028EF0`'s two values are produced by one conditional expression;
there is no statement to move, and every reordering the randomizer can reach
changes the instruction stream rather than the allocation.

So the wave-37 rule ("the permuter is **not** useless on register allocation —
order-wrong and slot-wrong are precisely its cases") stands, but narrow it:
**it needs two independently-schedulable definitions to permute.** Before
spending 300 s, check that the two values in the swap are defined by separate
statements. If they are two arms of one `?:` or one `if/else`, spend the time on
the reference count of the operands instead.

## fold() reassociates `n + 1 + f()` too — only a STATEMENT BOUNDARY after the call keeps `(n + 1) + f()` (wave 52, W52-D)

The wave-35 (W35-A) finding that agbcc's `fold()` reassociates `A - (B - K)`
unconditionally holds on a PLUS with a call, and the emitted code is the same
length either way, so the diff shows two `add`s that look transposed for no
reason.

`sub_0805E440`'s ROM has `bl Div / adds r1,r5,#1 / adds r1,r1,r0`, i.e.
`(n + 1) + q`. Measured in one `compile_probe`, four spellings:

| source                                            | emitted |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ------- |
| `n + 1 + Div(...)`                                 | `add rQ,rQ,#1 / add rN,rN,rQ`  — `n + (q + 1)` |
| `Div(...) + (n + 1)`                               | same |
| `q = Div(...); return n + 1 + q;`                  | same |
| `q = Div(...); t = n + 1; return t + q;`           | `add rN,rN,#1 / add rN,rN,rQ` — **the ROM** |

So parentheses do not stop `associate_trees`, and neither does binding the
call's result — only splitting the constant's addition into its OWN statement
does. The statement has to sit AFTER the call's statement: written before it,
the `add #1` is emitted ahead of the `bl` and the diff moves rather than closes.

## A value masked TWICE must NOT be bound to a local — the thumb `ands` ties whichever operand DIES (wave 52, W52-D)

`sub_0805E5AC` reads one map byte and masks it twice (`& 0xe0` for a compare,
`& 0x1f` for a table subscript). Bound to a local it lands at 98.6% with FIVE
bytes wrong, all in the second `ands`:

    ROM        movs r0,#0x1f / ands r0,r2      <- CONSTANT tied, cell preserved
    local      movs r1,#0x1f / ands r2,r1      <- cell tied, and clobbered

Thumb's `andsi3` marks operand 1 `%0`, so the tied operand becomes the
destination, and reload ties the one that is DEAD at the insn. A local's last
use dies there; a CSE substitution of a re-written expression does not. Writing
the map-byte expression out TWICE and leaving CSE to merge the loads restores
the ROM's form and matched.

Two controls that make this a measurement rather than a guess:

- Adding an artificial later use of the local (a trailing `return t;`) flips the
  tie back to the ROM's form exactly — confirming liveness is the variable — but
  costs a copy at the load, so it is a diagnostic, not a fix.
- Binding the MASK instead (`n = t & 0x1f`, with or without the assignment
  folded into the subscript as `tbl[n = t & 0x1f]`) does NOT work: it moves the
  `ands` ahead of the table's pool `ldr`.

**This is the exact inverse of `sub_0805E87C` in the same batch**, where the unit
id *needs* a local precisely to get its `adds r1,r0,#0` copy. The discriminator
is what the value feeds: a value feeding two MASKS wants no local, a value
feeding a POINTER MULTIPLY wants one.

Smaller readout from the same probe: the first guard's pool `ldr` lands between
`movs r0,#0xe0` and the `ands` only when the cell value is NARROW (`u8`,
QImode). With an `int` local it lands after the `ands`. Same length, no hint in
the diff.

## A CSE copy's POSITION is set by which STATEMENT the assignment belongs to (wave 52, W52-D)

Wave 27 (W27-A) established that an unexplained `adds rD,rS,#0` is a second
local holding a copy of the first. `sub_0805E87C` and `sub_0805E5AC` add where
it lands. Both have the ROM sequence

    ldrb r0,[r1] / cmp r0,#0 / beq ... / ldr r2,=gUnknown_08499594 / adds r1,r0,#0 / <*12> / ldr r1,[r2] / adds r5,r1,r0

— the pool `ldr` BEFORE the copy. Written as two statements
(`id = cell; u = g + id;`) the copy appears but lands BEFORE the pool `ldr`.
Folding the assignment into the pointer's own expression,
`u = gUnknown_08499594 + (id = cell)`, puts it after, and that is the match.
`id` is never read again in either function; the local exists only to create the
copy.

In `sub_0805E87C` this also fixed the indirect call four statements later:
with the copy missing, `gUnknown_030013EC`'s pool `ldr` sank below
`gUnknown_030040D8`'s and the two `.rodata` pool words swapped. Binding the
function pointer (`f = gUnknown_030013EC; f(...)`) fixes the pool order on its
own but then emits the pointer's LOAD before the arguments where the ROM sinks
it — a closer-looking spelling that is wrong. Another instance of "a change in a
loop flips an allocation in the tail".

## The 0x0816DA5C-0x0816DA84 run is an `-fforce-addr` pool block, confirmed word by word (wave 52, W52-D)

Dereferenced in `baserom.gba`, every word in the run holds a RAM or ROM address
and none of them is an object:

    0816DA5C 08499590   0816DA60 030040D8   0816DA64 030013EC
    0816DA6C 030040D8   0816DA70 08499590
    0816DA74 08499590   0816DA78 030040D8
    0816DA80 03003F20   0816DA84 030040D8

Four functions, private copies each, three symbols between them — the splitter's
`gUnknown_0816DAxx` names are pool words, not globals. All four matched with the
honest spelling and `try_match` reported
`relocs: name different symbols that resolve to the same address` on every one.
`0816DA88`/`0816DA8C` hold `0805E87D`/`0805E779`, THUMB function pointers, so the
pool block ENDS at 0816DA84 and a real table begins there.

Also visible across all four: only the FIRST reference to a symbol in a function
gets the force-addr word; later references in the same function take ordinary
inline pool words. The honest spelling reproduces that split by itself — do not
try to force every reference through the `.rodata` word.

## Two globals whose ADDRESS DIFFERENCE the ROM folds are ONE symbol (wave 53, W53-A)

`sub_08047C04` holds `gUnknown_02010450` in r4 and then reaches
`gUnknown_0200FC50` with

```
ldr r2, _08047E7C   @ =0xFFFFF800
adds r4, r4, r2
```

agbcc's address CSE can only compute the difference of two address constants at
compile time when they are the **same symbol** — two distinct `extern`s have no
known relationship, and a draft spelling them separately emits a fresh
`ldr rN, =gUnknown_0200FC50` there instead. So the subtraction is a **proof of
identity**, not a peephole: 0x02010450 is `gUnknown_0200FC50 + 0x800` and (from
the same function) 0x0200FE50 is `gUnknown_0200FC50 + 0x200`.

This is the strongest form of the brief's warning that nearby globals may be one
record. It is worth checking wherever a function loads two `gUnknown_` addresses
in the same region, because the payoff is larger than the one instruction:

- Three separate symbols with 5 references to the first one made agbcc emit a
  `-fforce-addr` `.rodata` word for it and burn a callee-saved register holding
  the word's address. One symbol with thirteen references emitted **no** pool
  word at all, because the references chain off one another instead of being
  live across the whole body. Read backwards: **a force-addr word in your draft
  on a function whose ROM has none can mean you have split one object into
  several, not that you have register pressure.**
- The offsets stop looking arbitrary. Against one base every access in that
  function pairs at +0x400 — 0x100/0x500, 0x200/0x600, 0x240/0x640,
  0x2c0/0x6c0, 0x800/0xc00, 0x880/0xc80 — a front/back double buffer, which
  three unrelated buffers do not explain.

`try_match` then prints `relocs: name different symbols that resolve to the same
address`, which is a match. Leave the other spelling declared if promoted files
already use it; the emitted word is identical.

## `x == 0 ? A : B` is FOLDED and inverted; the if/else STATEMENT is not (wave 53, W53-A)

`fold` rewrites `(x == 0) ? A : B` as `x ? B : A`, so the `?:` spelling emits
`beq` to an out-of-line `A`. The ROM shape

```
cmp r0, #0
bne  Lelse
<A>
b    Lend
Lelse: <B>
Lend:
```

is only reachable from the statement form:

```c
if (a->unk21 == 0)
    v = a->unk21;
else
    v = a->unk1f + 1;
```

Two further things that spelling settles, both of which cost an attempt each:

- **The zero arm is `v = a->unk21`, not `v = 0`.** The ROM has
  `adds r3, r0, #0` — a copy of the just-tested byte, known zero on that path.
  CSE will not turn a `const_int 0` into that copy on its own (const 0 is not
  more expensive than a register), so the *source* has to name the value. Read
  backwards: **a register copy where a constant would do means the source
  reused the tested expression.**
- **The condition being a statement moves the call's other arguments after the
  merge.** With the `?:` inside the argument list, agbcc evaluated argument 3
  (`ldr r2, [r6]`) *before* the branch; the ROM evaluates it after. Nothing
  about the branch itself distinguishes the two — the argument placement does.

## A bare pointer-cast lvalue is not `MEM_IN_STRUCT_P`, and it costs a RELOAD (wave 53, W53-A)

`sub_0804A260` clears six consecutive halfwords through a global pointer. Five
are ordinary members; the sixth sits at an offset the shared struct declares as
`u8` + filler, so the obvious spelling is
`*(s16 *)&gUnknown_030044E0->unk1e = 0;`. That spelling **reloads the global
pointer afterwards**:

```
ldr r0, [r6]
mov r4, #0
strh r4, [r0, #0x1e]
ldr r0, [r6]          @ <-- the ROM does not have this
mov r3, #0
strh r3, [r0, #0x20]
```

A MEM built by casting a pointer is not marked `MEM_IN_STRUCT_P`, so agbcc must
assume it aliases the pointer variable itself. Casting the *pointer* to a
struct that declares the member at the right offset and width keeps the flag,
